lessons.title: Family Forms and Family Diversity
lessons.description: Nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent, single sex, cohabiting and beanpole families, plus global forms.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Family?

There is no single, universally agreed definition of a family in sociology. Rather than adopting one definition as correct, sociologists study the variety of household and kinship arrangements that people live in and the social meanings attached to them. The UK is home to a wide range of family diversity — different family forms that have become increasingly common since the mid-twentieth century. Understanding each form factually, without privileging one as “normal”, is a core sociological skill.

Family Forms in the UK

Sociologists identify the following family forms as present in contemporary Britain:

  • Nuclear family: two parents and their dependent children living together. Functionalists such as Parsons argued this is the most efficient family form for modern industrial society, as it is geographically mobile and suited to the demands of the labour market.
  • Extended family: a family network beyond the nuclear unit, including grandparents and other relatives. Extended families may be vertically extended (three or more generations) or horizontally extended (relatives of the same generation).
  • Reconstituted family: also called a blended family, formed when two adults — at least one of whom has children from a previous relationship — form a new household. Reconstituted families have grown as divorce and repartnering have become more common.
  • Lone parent family: one parent living with and caring for dependent children without a resident partner. ONS data shows around one in four families with dependent children in the UK is a lone parent family; the majority of lone parents are women.
  • Single sex (same-sex) family: a family in which both parents are of the same sex. The Civil Partnership Act 2004 and the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 gave same-sex couples in the UK formal legal recognition.
  • Cohabiting family: a couple — same-sex or different-sex — living together without being married or in a civil partnership. Cohabitation has grown significantly in the UK since the 1970s.
  • Beanpole family: a multi-generational family that is tall and narrow. Declining birth rates mean fewer children in each generation, while increased life expectancy means more generations are alive at the same time. The beanpole family has strong vertical ties (grandparents — parents — grandchildren) but fewer horizontal ties (siblings, cousins).
Key Fact

The GCSE Sociology specification identifies seven family forms in the UK: nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent, single sex, cohabiting and beanpole. Each describes a different household arrangement. Sociologists study all of them as legitimate family forms without treating any one as the correct or “normal” version.

Ethnic Minority Family Forms

Within the UK, ethnic minority communities often have distinct patterns of family organisation. South Asian families, for example, may maintain stronger extended kinship networks than the White British average, with grandparents playing a prominent role in child rearing and family decision making. African-Caribbean families have historically had higher rates of lone parent households, reflecting a complex mix of historical, economic and cultural factors. Sociologists emphasise that these patterns should be understood in their social and economic context rather than pathologised. Religious beliefs also shape family practices: Muslim, Hindu, Jewish and Sikh families may organise marriage, gender roles and household arrangements differently in accordance with their faith traditions.

Global Family Forms

Family forms differ not only within the UK but across the world. The specification explicitly names several global examples that students should understand:

  • Polygamy: marriage to more than one spouse simultaneously. Polygyny (one man, multiple wives) is practised in some parts of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia. Polyandry (one woman, multiple husbands) is rare but found in some communities in Nepal and Tibet. Both are illegal in the UK.
  • Arranged marriages: in arranged marriage systems, the families of both partners take a leading role in identifying a suitable match, though in contemporary practice the individuals concerned typically have the right to accept or refuse. This differs from forced marriage, which is illegal in the UK and is not the same as arranged marriage.

China’s one-child family policy, introduced in 1979 and largely in force until 2015, is the most prominent example of state policy directly determining family structure. Couples in urban areas were limited to one child, with financial penalties for additional children. The policy had significant sociological consequences: it produced the so-called “4-2-1” family structure (four grandparents, two parents, one child), created demographic imbalances (sex-selective practices resulted in far more boys than girls in some regions), and placed enormous financial pressure on single children to support elderly parents in later life.

China’s case illustrates that family forms are not only shaped by culture and individual choice but can be directly engineered by political and economic forces. This challenges any assumption that family structure is purely natural or traditional. The policy was ended in 2015 (a two-child policy was introduced, then expanded to three children in 2021) in response to an ageing population and declining birth rate — demonstrating that state intervention in family formation creates its own long-term social consequences.

Key Fact

Global family forms include polygamy (polygyny and polyandry), arranged marriages and state-shaped family structures such as China’s one-child policy. These demonstrate that family forms are socially and politically constructed rather than naturally universal — a key sociological argument against assuming the nuclear family is the only valid form.

Sociologists disagree about what the growth of family diversity means for British society. The New Right, associated with Murray, views the growth of lone parent families and cohabitation with concern, arguing that the breakdown of the traditional nuclear family is linked to social problems including poverty, crime and educational underachievement. Murray argued that lone parent households contribute to a dependency culture and the development of an underclass.

Feminist sociologists, by contrast, tend to view the growth of family diversity as reflecting women’s greater economic independence and freedom to leave unhappy marriages and partnerships. From a feminist perspective, the decline of the traditional nuclear family represents progress rather than crisis. Postmodernist sociologists argue that diversity and individual choice are defining features of contemporary life and that no single family form can be presented as superior to others.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On a 3-mark Identify and Describe question about family forms, identify the specific form clearly (1 mark) and then develop your description with at least one further defining feature and either a relevant statistic, an example or a sociological link (2 marks). For example: “A beanpole family is a multi-generational family that is tall and narrow — declining birth rates mean fewer siblings and cousins in each generation, while increased life expectancy means three or four generations are alive simultaneously, creating strong vertical ties between grandparents, parents and grandchildren.” A common mistake is stopping after one sentence, which earns only 1 mark.

On a 12-mark Evaluate question about family diversity, never assert that one family form is better or worse than another — that is the New Right’s position, not an authorial claim. Present the New Right, feminist and postmodernist views as competing perspectives, name Murray and at least one feminist sociologist (Oakley), and reach a supported conclusion that weighs the evidence. Students who only describe family forms without engaging with perspectives cap well below the Mastering band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The GCSE Sociology specification identifies seven UK family forms: nuclear, extended, reconstituted, lone parent, single sex, cohabiting and beanpole. Each describes a different household arrangement, and sociologists study all without privileging one as normal.
  • Global family forms include polygamy (polygyny and polyandry), arranged marriages and state-shaped family structures such as China’s one-child policy — showing that family forms are socially constructed rather than naturally universal.
  • Perspectives on family diversity differ: the New Right (Murray) views the growth of lone parent families and cohabitation as linked to social problems; feminist sociologists see it as reflecting women’s growing independence; postmodernist sociologists celebrate diversity and individual choice as defining features of contemporary life.

lessons.title: Social Change and Family Structures
lessons.description: How secularisation, feminism and economic change reshaped family diversity in modern Britain.
lessons.content_html:
Why Has Family Structure Changed?

Since the mid-twentieth century, the range of family diversity in the UK has grown significantly. The nuclear family — two parents and their dependent children — remains the most common form according to ONS data, but the proportion of lone parent families, cohabiting couples and reconstituted families has grown substantially. Sociologists identify several interconnected drivers of this change. Understanding them as a set of causes, rather than listing them in isolation, is the key to top-band answers on this topic.

Drivers of Change in Family Structure

The specification identifies five key drivers of change in family forms. Each has reshaped both the structure of households and the norms attached to family life:

Secularisation refers to the long-term decline in the social influence of religion. The Church of England and the Roman Catholic Church traditionally taught that marriage was a lifelong sacrament and that divorce, cohabitation and same-sex partnerships were morally wrong. As church attendance fell across the twentieth century, religious authority over personal and family decisions weakened. Cohabitation, previously stigmatised, became socially mainstream. Divorce became more acceptable. By the early twenty-first century, same-sex partnerships were legally recognised through the Civil Partnership Act 2004 and the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 — changes that would have been unthinkable in a highly religious society.

Feminist movements of the 1960s and 1970s challenged the expectation that women should primarily be wives and mothers. Legal changes followed: the Equal Pay Act 1970 and Sex Discrimination Act 1975 expanded women’s access to paid employment and economic independence. As women gained greater financial autonomy, they became less dependent on marriage for economic security. This contributed to a rise in both cohabitation (as women delayed or avoided marriage) and divorce (as women were able to leave unsatisfactory marriages). The growth of lone parent families — the large majority headed by women — is partly explained by women’s greater capacity to live independently. Ann Oakley and feminist sociologists argued that these changes represented progress away from the patriarchal conventional family.

Economic factors shape family formation in significant ways. The growth of dual career families — where both partners are in paid employment — reflects both feminist gains in the labour market and economic necessity (rising housing costs in many parts of the UK have made a single income insufficient). Conversely, economic inequality and poverty reduce the options available to families. Young adults who cannot afford independent housing may delay family formation, contributing to later ages of first marriage and first parenthood. High housing costs have also driven the growth of “boomerang children” — adult children who return to the parental home after university or following relationship breakdown.

Technological change has reshaped family formation in two main ways. First, the widespread availability of reliable contraception since the 1960s separated sex from reproduction, making cohabitation and non-marital relationships less likely to result in unplanned pregnancies. This contributed directly to the normalisation of cohabitation and to declining birth rates and smaller family sizes. Second, digital communication technologies have transformed how extended family networks stay connected across geographical distances — what sociologists call the “connected family” — maintaining emotional ties across dispersed family forms.

Post-war immigration, particularly from South Asia, the Caribbean and more recently Eastern Europe, has diversified family forms in the UK. South Asian communities often maintain stronger extended kinship networks and a greater emphasis on arranged marriages than the White British average. African-Caribbean communities have higher rates of lone parent households. These differences should be understood sociologically — they reflect distinct cultural traditions, historical experiences and economic conditions, not family dysfunction. Migration itself can also disrupt family forms, creating transnational families in which members live across different countries.

The Rapoports: Five Types of Family Diversity

Rhona and Robert Rapoport argued that British society is characterised by diversity rather than a single dominant family form. Rather than simply counting different household structures, they identified five distinct dimensions of family diversity in their 1982 analysis — showing that diversity runs far deeper than structure alone:

  • Organisational diversity: differences in the way families divide paid and unpaid work. For example, dual career families versus families with a traditional breadwinner-homemaker split.
  • Cultural diversity: differences related to ethnicity and religion. South Asian families in the UK may maintain stronger extended kinship networks; Muslim, Hindu or Jewish families may organise marriage and gender roles differently.
  • Social class diversity: working-class and middle-class families differ in income, housing, parenting styles and the opportunities available to children.
  • Life cycle diversity: family structure changes across an individual’s life — a young childless couple, a family with young children, a beanpole family with elderly grandparents and a lone individual are all at different life cycle stages.
  • Cohort diversity: people born in different generations have experienced different historical conditions. Attitudes to divorce, cohabitation and same-sex partnerships differ markedly between older and younger cohorts.
Key Fact

The Rapoports (1982) identified five types of family diversity in Britain: organisational, cultural, social class, life cycle and cohort. These show that family diversity is not simply about different household structures — it runs through differences in work patterns, ethnicity, social class, life stage and generational experience.

Trends in Family Change: Divorce, Cohabitation and Singlehood

Several statistical trends illustrate how family structures have changed in Britain since the 1970s. Divorce rates rose dramatically after the Divorce Reform Act 1969, peaking in the 1990s before declining somewhat (partly because fewer people are marrying in the first place). Cohabitation has grown from a small minority of couples in the 1970s to a common arrangement today. The age of first marriage has risen steadily: in 1970 the average age of first marriage was in the mid-twenties; by the 2020s it had risen to the early thirties. Singlehood — living alone, either by choice or circumstance — has also increased, driven by both higher divorce rates and a trend towards later partnership formation. Serial monogamy — a succession of committed relationships — has become more common as remarriage rates remain significant.

Key Fact

Key trends since 1970: divorce rates rose then plateaued; cohabitation has grown significantly; age of first marriage has risen; family size has shrunk; singlehood has increased. These trends are interlinked — fewer marriages means fewer divorces; later marriage means more cohabitation; greater economic independence for women drives both cohabitation and divorce rises.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On a 4-mark Describe question about changes in family structure, organise your answer around causes rather than trends alone. The specification expects you to explain why family forms have changed, not just that they have. One mark per identified cause with a developed description is the typical pattern: secularisation (declining religious stigma), feminism (women’s economic independence), economic factors (dual career families, housing costs) and changing laws are the four most creditworthy causes.

On a 9-mark Discuss question about the Rapoports or family diversity, always name the Rapoports explicitly (“Rhona and Robert Rapoport argued in 1982 that…”) and link their five types to at least one broader perspective on family diversity. The New Right view (Murray) and the feminist view (Oakley) provide the contrast that earns the “both sides” marks. Students who list five Rapoport types but add no perspective-based evaluation stay in the Developing band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Five key drivers of change in family structure are: secularisation (declining religious stigma against cohabitation and divorce), feminism and the changing status of women, economic factors (dual career families, housing costs), technological change (contraception, digital communication) and immigration (diversifying UK family forms).
  • The Rapoports (1982) identified five types of family diversity in Britain: organisational, cultural, social class, life cycle and cohort. These show that diversity is deeper than just household structure — it runs through work patterns, ethnicity, class, life stage and generational experience.
  • Statistical trends since the 1970s include: rising divorce rates (peaking 1990s), growth of cohabitation, a rising age of first marriage, smaller family sizes and increasing singlehood. These trends are interconnected and reflect the broader social changes described by the drivers above.

lessons.title: Social Change and Family Relationships
lessons.description: Conjugal roles, the domestic division of labour and how family relationships changed in modern Britain.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Conjugal Roles?

Conjugal roles refer to the roles performed by each partner within a couple relationship. Sociologists distinguish between two broad patterns. Joint conjugal roles describe partnerships where tasks, decision making and leisure are shared between partners. Segregated conjugal roles describe partnerships where male and female partners have clearly defined separate tasks — typically, the man in paid employment and the woman in domestic work and child rearing. Understanding how these patterns have changed — and whether they have genuinely become more equal — is at the heart of the families and relationships topic.

The Domestic Division of Labour

The domestic division of labour refers to how unpaid household tasks and child rearing are distributed within the home. Sociologists study a wide range of activities: cooking, cleaning, laundry, child care, disciplining children, managing household finances, arranging leisure activities and making major household decisions. The central question is whether this division is equal between partners, and whether it has become more equal as women have entered the paid workforce in greater numbers.

Functionalist View: Parsons and Complementary Roles

Talcott Parsons argued that the gender-divided conjugal role pattern — the man performing the instrumental role (breadwinner, financial provider) and the woman performing the expressive role (homemaker, emotional carer) — was both functionally efficient and naturally grounded. From this perspective, segregated conjugal roles are complementary: each partner contributes different but equally important tasks. Parsons presented this division as meeting the needs of modern industrial society, where paid employment demands geographical mobility and one adult must maintain the home while the other moves with work.

Peter Willmott and Michael Young (1973) argued that conjugal roles were becoming more equal over time. Their research suggested the modern family was becoming “symmetrical” — meaning that partners were increasingly sharing domestic tasks and leisure. Willmott and Young described the symmetrical family as one where roles are not identical but broadly equal in the time and effort each partner contributes. They linked this change to the principle of stratified diffusion: lifestyle changes begin among middle-class families and gradually spread to working-class families. For Willmott and Young, the trend towards symmetry represented a positive “march of progress” in family life.

Oakley’s Feminist Critique: The Myth of the Symmetrical Family

Ann Oakley directly challenged Willmott and Young’s optimistic picture. Her research on housework, published in The Sociology of Housework (1974), found that the domestic division of labour remained profoundly unequal despite changes in women’s employment. Oakley argued that the conventional family — with its gender-divided roles — was not disappearing but persisting in new forms. She criticised Willmott and Young’s methodology, noting that their threshold for male domestic participation was very low: men who helped with housework at least once a week were counted as “participating”.

Oakley developed the concept of the double shift to describe the burden on women who work in paid employment but continue to perform the majority of domestic labour at home. Rather than replacing domestic work, women’s entry into the paid labour market added a second shift to their day. Some feminist sociologists have further extended this to the concept of the triple shift — paid work, domestic labour and the emotional management of family relationships — capturing the full range of labour that women typically carry out.

Key Fact

Willmott and Young (1973) argued that conjugal roles were becoming more equal through the “symmetrical family” and the principle of stratified diffusion. Oakley challenged this as a myth — her research showed the domestic division of labour remained unequal and that women performed a “double shift” of paid work plus domestic labour.

Contemporary Issues: Dual Career Families, Decision Making and Leisure

Dual career families — where both partners are in paid employment — have grown significantly. This raises questions about how domestic labour is redistributed when both partners work. Research consistently shows that even in dual career households, women perform more domestic tasks and child care than their male partners on average. Decision making — who has the final say on major financial or household decisions — continues to be gendered in many households, with men retaining greater influence over major financial decisions. Money management patterns vary: in some families one partner controls all finances; in others both have independent access to income. Leisure activities also differ: research suggests men have more free leisure time than women in couples, where women’s leisure is more frequently interrupted by domestic and caring responsibilities.

Child-Centred Families, Boomerang Children and the Sandwich Generation

The specification identifies three further concepts about how family relationships have changed:

  • Child-centred families: post-war British families became increasingly organised around the needs and wellbeing of children. Children’s emotional development, education and leisure became central concerns of parenting. This represents a significant shift from earlier generations in which children were expected to contribute economically to the household from a young age.
  • Boomerang children: adult children who return to the parental home after living independently, typically due to high housing costs, unemployment or relationship breakdown. High property prices in many parts of the UK have made this trend particularly pronounced, with many people in their twenties and thirties unable to afford to live independently.
  • Sandwich generation: people in middle age who face the dual responsibility of caring for both their own (sometimes adult) children and their ageing parents at the same time. The combination of extended life expectancy and delayed childbearing has made this “squeezed middle” experience more common. The caring burden falls disproportionately on women.
Key Fact

The boomerang generation (adult children returning home due to housing costs) and the sandwich generation (middle-aged adults caring for both children and parents simultaneously) are two contemporary features of British family life that reflect both economic pressures and demographic change. Both tend to increase the caring burden on women.

The “New Man” — the idea of a modern father who shares fully in domestic tasks and child rearing — is frequently cited in media and everyday discussion as evidence that conjugal roles have become equal. Feminist sociologists challenge this. Oakley argued that media representations of involved fatherhood are not backed by empirical data: the domestic division of labour remains unequal across most households. More men take paternity leave than in previous generations, but research suggests the distribution of daily, routine domestic tasks (cooking, cleaning, laundry, managing children’s schedules) continues to fall disproportionately on women. The “New Man” may be a cultural ideal rather than a sociological reality.

A full answer: “The double shift refers to the situation in which women in paid employment also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home, effectively working two shifts in a day.”

On a 12-mark Evaluate about conjugal roles, the highest marks are earned by presenting the Willmott and Young symmetrical family argument AND Oakley’s feminist counter, then adding a third perspective (Parsons’ functionalist complementary roles argument or the Marxist feminist view that domestic labour benefits capitalism). Students who describe the debate but reach no supported conclusion stay in the Secure band. lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Conjugal roles describe how partners divide paid work, domestic tasks and child rearing. Joint conjugal roles are relatively equal; segregated conjugal roles assign distinct tasks by gender. The domestic division of labour includes decision making, money management, child rearing, household tasks and leisure.
  • Willmott and Young (1973) argued the family was becoming symmetrical through the principle of stratified diffusion. Oakley challenged this as a myth — her research showed the domestic division of labour remained unequal and that women performed a double shift (and sometimes a triple shift) of paid work, domestic labour and emotional management.
  • Contemporary trends include child-centred families, boomerang children (returning home due to housing costs) and the sandwich generation (caring for both children and ageing parents). These trends tend to place additional caring burdens on women, supporting Oakley’s argument that gender inequality in the home persists.

lessons.title: Sociological Theories of the Role of the Family
lessons.description: Functionalist, Marxist, feminist and New Right theories of the family’s role in society.
lessons.content_html:
The Conflict versus Consensus Debate

One of the defining debates in GCSE Sociology is between consensus perspectives, which argue that social institutions like the family benefit society as a whole, and conflict perspectives, which argue that the family primarily serves the interests of powerful groups at the expense of others. Functionalism represents the consensus view; Marxism, feminism and the New Right each offer different conflict analyses. Understanding this debate — and being able to present each perspective with named sociologists — is central to the families unit.

Functionalist Theory of the Family: Parsons

Talcott Parsons argued that in modern industrial societies the family performs two irreducible functions that no other institution can perform as effectively. First, the primary socialisation of children — instilling the shared norms and values that allow individuals to participate in society. Second, the stabilisation of adult personalities. Parsons described this as the “warm bath” effect: the family provides emotional comfort and psychological stability for adult members, releasing the tensions that accumulate in the competitive world of paid work.

Parsons argued that the instrumental role (performed by the husband/father — breadwinner, financial provider) and the expressive role (performed by the wife/mother — emotional nurturer, homemaker) are biologically grounded and functionally necessary. He presented these as complementary: different but equally important. From a functionalist perspective, the nuclear family with gender-divided roles is the most efficient unit for meeting society’s needs.

Key Fact

Parsons argued the family has two irreducible functions: (1) primary socialisation — teaching children the norms and values needed to participate in society; (2) stabilisation of adult personalities — the “warm bath” of emotional comfort that releases tensions from paid work. The instrumental role (breadwinner) is performed by the male partner; the expressive role (emotional carer) is performed by the female partner.

Marxist Theory of the Family: Zaretsky

Marxist sociologists argue that the family serves the interests of capitalism rather than society as a whole. Eli Zaretsky (1976) argued that the family under capitalism performs two key functions for the bourgeoisie. First, it reproduces the labour force — workers raise the next generation of workers at their own expense, subsidising capitalism’s need for a continuing workforce. Second, it acts as an emotional refuge: Parsons’s “warm bath” is, for Zaretsky, a mechanism that stabilises capitalism by absorbing workers’ discontent. Workers who experience alienation and exploitation at work are directed to seek fulfilment in family life, reducing the likelihood of collective resistance.

Zaretsky also argued that the family functions as a unit of consumption — purchasing the goods and services that generate profit for the bourgeoisie. The home filled with consumer goods (appliances, food, clothing, entertainment) represents a major market for capitalist industry. From this perspective, the cultural celebration of home and family life serves the interests of capitalism rather than genuinely meeting workers’ needs. The family also performs an ideological function: it presents existing social arrangements as natural and permanent, discouraging challenge to the capitalist order.

Christine Delphy and Diana Leonard developed a structural feminist critique of the family that went beyond individual men behaving badly. They argued that the family is best understood as a patriarchal economic institution — one in which the husband is the head and primary beneficiary of all work performed within the household. Women’s domestic labour — cooking, cleaning, child rearing, emotional support, nursing the sick — is systematically exploited by men, who benefit from these services without equivalent compensation. This is not a matter of individual relationships but of a structural arrangement in which men as a group benefit from women’s unpaid work.

Delphy and Leonard also argued that women’s position within the family keeps them economically dependent, reducing their capacity to challenge patriarchal arrangements. What Murdock called the “economic function” of the family is, from Delphy and Leonard’s perspective, a system in which women’s labour is extracted for men’s benefit under the guise of love and care.

Feminist Theory of the Family: Oakley

Ann Oakley challenged the functionalist picture from a feminist direction. She argued that the conventional family — with its gendered division of labour — is not a natural arrangement but a socially constructed one that disadvantages women. What Parsons presented as the “expressive role” is, in practice, unpaid domestic labour that women perform while men benefit from the financial returns of the “instrumental role”. Oakley’s concept of the double shift captures the additional burden on women who enter paid employment: rather than the domestic division of labour adjusting, women simply acquire a second shift of work on top of domestic responsibilities.

Key Fact

Three perspectives compete on the role of the family: functionalists (Parsons) see it as performing essential functions benefiting all of society; Marxists (Zaretsky) see it as serving capitalism by reproducing the workforce and absorbing discontent; feminists (Oakley; Delphy and Leonard) see it as serving men’s interests through women’s unpaid labour in a patriarchal structure.

New Right Theory of the Family

The New Right perspective, associated with Charles Murray, shares the functionalist view that the nuclear family is the most beneficial family form but adds a political critique of family change. Murray argued that the growth of lone parent families, cohabitation and family breakdown has contributed to the development of an underclass — a group dependent on state benefits, disconnected from mainstream society and passing this lifestyle on to the next generation. The New Right argues that the welfare state has inadvertently made it economically rational for women to raise children alone, removing the incentive for male responsibility within the family.

The New Right view is criticised by feminist sociologists, who argue it pathologises lone parent families without recognising the structural causes of their difficulties (poverty, the gender pay gap, lack of affordable child care). From a feminist perspective, the New Right’s concern is really about restoring male authority within the family rather than genuinely addressing poverty or social inequality.

A common error is treating the functions of the family as a neutral list that all perspectives accept. In fact, while Parsons describes the family’s functions positively (it meets real social needs), Marxists and feminists fundamentally challenge whose needs are being served. Feminists point out that the “expressive role” disguises unpaid female labour. Marxists argue the “economic function” involves reproducing the workforce and consuming capitalist products. The New Right endorses the functionalist picture but adds a political critique of state welfare. The same activities can be described very differently depending on which theoretical starting point you adopt — this is exactly the kind of perspectival comparison that earns marks in the 9-mark and 12-mark questions.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On a 12-mark Evaluate question about theories of the family, the most common mistake is presenting only the functionalist view (Parsons) and stopping there. The mark scheme explicitly rewards candidates who present the functionalist case AND at least two contrasting perspectives. Name your sociologists precisely: “Zaretsky argued that…”, “Delphy and Leonard contended that…”, “Murray’s New Right view holds that…”. The conflict versus consensus debate is the structural frame your answer needs — always signal which side of the debate each sociologist falls on.

On a 2-mark Define question for “primary socialisation”, include two elements: (1) it is the earliest stage of socialisation and (2) it occurs within the family. Writing only “learning norms and values” without specifying the family as the agent earns 1 mark, not 2.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Parsons (functionalist) argued the family has two irreducible functions: primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personalities (“warm bath” theory). The instrumental role (male breadwinner) and expressive role (female carer) are complementary and functionally necessary.
  • Zaretsky (Marxist) argued the family serves capitalism: it reproduces the workforce, absorbs worker discontent, acts as a unit of consumption and performs an ideological function. Delphy and Leonard and Oakley (feminist) argue the family serves men’s interests through women’s unpaid domestic labour in a patriarchal structure.
  • Murray’s New Right perspective views family diversity, particularly lone parent families, as contributing to an underclass and dependency culture. Feminist sociologists challenge this, arguing it pathologises lone parent families without addressing the structural causes of poverty.

lessons.title: Criticisms of the Family
lessons.description: The dark side of family life: criticisms, conflict, domestic violence and the myth of the happy home.
lessons.content_html:
Why Is the Family Criticised?

While functionalist sociologists emphasise the positive functions the family performs, a range of other perspectives offer sustained critiques of family life. These critiques come from different directions: some focus on structural problems with the family as an institution; others point to the gap between the idealised image of family life and its lived reality. Understanding these criticisms — and the competing perspectives behind them — is essential for extended response questions on this topic.

Loss of Traditional Functions

Sociologists have noted that many functions once performed within the family have been transferred to external institutions. Economic production, religious instruction, health care and education have been taken over by employers, schools, the NHS and the state. Parsons acknowledged this and argued the family adapted by specialising in primary socialisation and personality stabilisation. Critics, however, argue that this “loss of functions” has left the family with a reduced role, created uncertainty about its purpose and reduced its capacity to support members in practical ways. The family that was once a self-sufficient economic unit has become primarily a unit of consumption — dependent on market goods and state services rather than producing what it needs.

The Problem of Isolation

One prominent criticism of the modern nuclear family is that it has become socially isolated. As the nuclear family became more self-contained and home-centred — what sociologists sometimes call “privatised” — it lost contact with extended kinship networks and local communities. This isolation places enormous pressure on individual family members, particularly during times of crisis or stress. Without wider networks to share the burden, difficulties within the household can escalate. Critics argue that the isolated nuclear family is an emotionally intense unit that can generate conflict, mental health problems and domestic violence, rather than automatically providing the emotional refuge that Parsons described.

Unrealistic Idealisation of Family Life

A related criticism is the idealisation of family life. Advertising, popular culture and political discourse consistently portray the family as a place of unconditional love, safety and mutual support. Critics argue that this idealised image conceals the very real conflicts, inequalities and abuses that occur within families. The private nature of the family — what Parsons saw as one of its strengths — means that problems within it are hidden from public view and harder to address through social policy or intervention. Domestic violence, emotional abuse, child neglect and financial exploitation are all more likely to occur within family settings than between strangers, yet these realities are underrepresented in cultural portrayals of family life.

Dysfunctional families are those in which relationships cause harm rather than provide support. Sociologists use the term to describe families characterised by persistent conflict, domestic violence, substance abuse, neglect or emotional harm. The New Right (Murray) argues that growing family diversity — particularly the rise of lone parent families — has increased the prevalence of dysfunctional families and associated social problems including crime and educational underachievement. Feminist sociologists challenge this view, arguing that the concept of “dysfunctional family” is frequently used to pathologise lone parent families without recognising the structural causes of their difficulties: poverty, lack of affordable child care, the gender pay gap and inadequate social support.

Marital breakdown is a related concern. It can take the form of legal divorce, long-term separation, or an empty shell marriage — a marriage that persists formally but in which the couple have effectively ceased to have a meaningful relationship. The concept of the empty shell marriage is important because it shows that official divorce statistics undercount the true extent of marital breakdown: not all unhappy marriages end in legal divorce.

The Status and Role of Women in Families

Feminist sociologists have argued that the role and status of women within families is a key site of inequality. Ann Oakley argued that the role of women within families has been constructed around the expectation of unpaid domestic service. Women’s labour in the home — cooking, cleaning, child care, emotional management — is treated as natural and invisible rather than as skilled work with economic value. The conventional family, Oakley argued, is not a partnership of equals but a system in which women’s time and labour are taken for granted. Even as women have entered paid employment, the domestic division of labour has not adjusted proportionately — women acquire a double shift rather than gaining equality.

Key Fact

Key criticisms of the family include: social isolation of the nuclear family; unrealistic idealisation concealing conflict and abuse; loss of traditional functions; dysfunctional families; marital breakdown and empty shell marriages; and the inferior status and role of women through unpaid domestic labour. Feminist sociologists (Oakley) and the New Right (Murray) offer contrasting explanations of these problems.

The Dark Side of Family Life: Domestic Violence

The GCSE Sociology specification explicitly requires students to engage with the “dark side of family life”, including domestic violence. This is an important qualification to the functionalist “warm bath” view of the family as a safe and supportive environment. According to data from the Crime Survey for England and Wales, around 2.1 million adults experienced domestic abuse in the year to March 2023; the majority of victims are women. Domestic abuse includes physical violence, controlling behaviour, economic abuse, coercive control and psychological harm. It predominantly occurs within intimate partner and family relationships.

Feminist sociologists argue that domestic violence is not an individual or pathological problem but a structural one rooted in patriarchy. The family, as an institution, concentrates male authority over women and children in a private space that is difficult for the state to monitor or regulate. Ann Oakley and other feminist sociologists argue that domestic violence is a manifestation of patriarchal power relations, not a failure of the family as an ideal but evidence that the family as it is currently structured systematically disadvantages women. This is the sharpest feminist challenge to the functionalist view that the family benefits all its members equally.

Functionalists respond to these criticisms by arguing that critics focus on the dysfunctions of family life while undervaluing its genuine benefits. Murdock and Parsons maintained that the family performs necessary functions — particularly primary socialisation and personality stabilisation — that no other institution performs as effectively. While dysfunctional families clearly exist, functionalists argue these represent failures of the institution rather than evidence against the institution itself. The New Right (Murray) shares the functionalist endorsement of the nuclear family but attributes its problems to family diversity — particularly lone parent families — rather than to any inherent flaw in the family as a structure.

Key Fact

Feminist sociologists argue that domestic violence is a structural consequence of patriarchy within the family, not an individual aberration. Functionalists argue that dysfunctional families are failures of the institution, not evidence against it — the family still performs irreplaceable primary socialisation. The two perspectives fundamentally disagree about whether the family as an institution is the problem or the solution.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On a 9-mark Discuss question about criticisms of the family, the examiners reward answers that present the feminist critique (Oakley on the status of women; domestic violence as structural patriarchy) AND the functionalist defence (Parsons’ argument that dysfunctional families are failures of the institution, not evidence against it) alongside a supported judgement. A common mistake is listing criticisms without linking them to named perspectives or sociologists — this caps the answer in the Developing band even if the content is correct.

On a 2-mark Define question for “empty shell marriage”, include both components: (1) the marriage continues legally and (2) the emotional relationship has effectively ended. Describing it only as “an unhappy marriage” earns 1 mark at best — the sociological precision of “continues legally” is what earns the second mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Criticisms of families include: social isolation of the nuclear family; unrealistic idealisation concealing conflict and abuse; loss of traditional functions; dysfunctional families; marital breakdown; empty shell marriages; and the inferior status and role of women through the expectation of unpaid domestic service (Oakley).
  • The “dark side” of family life includes domestic violence, which feminist sociologists argue is a structural consequence of patriarchy. Crime Survey for England and Wales data shows approximately 2.1 million adults experienced domestic abuse in a single year. This directly challenges the functionalist “warm bath” view of the family as a safe refuge.
  • Functionalists argue dysfunctional families are failures of the institution, not evidence against it. The New Right (Murray) blames family diversity — particularly lone parent families — for social problems. Feminist sociologists reject both views, arguing the family’s problems are structural consequences of patriarchy.

lessons.title: Divorce: Causes, Consequences and Theoretical Perspectives
lessons.description: Why divorce rose in Britain: legal change, secularisation, women’s status, and consequences for families.
lessons.content_html:
Divorce in Britain Since 1945

Divorce is the legal ending of a marriage. The pattern of divorce in Britain since 1945 is one of dramatic and sustained increase, followed by a plateau and some decline in more recent years. In the decade after the Second World War, divorce was relatively rare — around 25,000 divorces per year in England and Wales. By the mid-1990s this had risen to around 175,000 per year. Since then the rate has declined somewhat, partly because marriage itself has become less common: more couples cohabit rather than marry, and fewer marriages can therefore end in divorce. Understanding the causes and consequences of this change is a central requirement of the families topic.

Legal Changes: The Divorce Reform Act 1969 and the 2022 No-Fault Reform

One of the most significant causes of the rising divorce rate was legal change. The Divorce Reform Act 1969, which came into force in 1971, fundamentally changed the legal basis of divorce in England and Wales. Before 1969, divorce required proof of a matrimonial “offence” such as adultery or cruelty. The 1969 Act replaced this with a single ground: irretrievable breakdown of marriage. This made divorce substantially easier and cheaper to obtain, and the divorce rate almost doubled in the years immediately after the Act came into force.

A further significant reform occurred in 2022 in England and Wales. The Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 (which came into force in April 2022) introduced no-fault divorce. Previously, even under the 1969 Act, one partner usually had to cite fault (such as adultery or unreasonable behaviour) to obtain a prompt divorce. The 2022 reform removed the need to attribute blame, making the process less adversarial. Sociologists note this reform may reduce the financial and psychological costs of divorce and could contribute to further changes in divorce statistics in the coming years.

Changing Social Attitudes and Secularisation

Legal change does not occur in a social vacuum. The 1969 Act reflected — and further accelerated — a broader shift in social attitudes towards divorce. As Britain became an increasingly secularised society, the religious stigma attached to divorce diminished. The Church of England and the Roman Catholic Church had traditionally taught that marriage was a lifelong sacrament and that divorce was morally wrong. As church attendance fell across the twentieth century and religious authority over personal life weakened, divorce became more socially acceptable. By the end of the twentieth century, divorce carried little social stigma in most communities.

More broadly, changing social values contributed to higher divorce rates. The growing expectation that marriage should provide personal fulfilment, romantic love and emotional intimacy — rather than simply economic partnership or social respectability — raised the bar for what constituted a “good enough” marriage. When marriages fell below this standard, individuals became more likely to seek divorce rather than continue in an unhappy relationship.

Key Fact

Four main reasons explain the rise in divorce since 1945: (1) legal change — the Divorce Reform Act 1969 introduced irretrievable breakdown as grounds for divorce; (2) the 2022 no-fault divorce reform reduced adversarial blame; (3) secularisation — declining religious stigma against divorce; (4) changing social attitudes and the changing status of women.

The Changing Status of Women

A particularly important cause of rising divorce rates is the changing status of women in society. Women’s increasing participation in paid employment since the Second World War gave many women greater economic independence. This reduced the financial dependence on a male partner that had previously made divorce an unviable option for many women. Research consistently shows that the majority of divorce petitions in England and Wales are filed by women — suggesting that women are more likely to seek to end unsatisfactory marriages when they have the economic means to do so.

The changing status of women is also linked to changing expectations: women’s greater social and political equality has raised their expectations of what a marriage should provide. The continued unequal distribution of domestic labour — Oakley’s double shift — means that many women experience marriage as disproportionately burdensome, and rising aspirations make this burden less acceptable over time.

Consequences of Divorce for Family Members

The consequences of divorce affect all members of the family. For partners, divorce can bring relief from an unhappy relationship but also significant emotional, financial and practical difficulties. Women tend to experience greater financial hardship after divorce, since they are more likely to have reduced their participation in paid employment during the marriage. Men tend to experience greater social isolation after divorce, since they are less likely to have primary care of children and may have weaker social networks outside the family.

For children, sociological research presents a complex picture. Some research suggests that parental conflict — not divorce itself — is the key factor in children’s outcomes. Divorce may in some cases be better for children than continuing in a highly conflicted marriage. Other research highlights the economic and social disadvantages associated with growing up in a lone parent household, including lower educational achievement and poorer health outcomes. Sociologists caution against treating all divorces as equally harmful, since outcomes vary significantly with income, quality of post-divorce parenting arrangements and the degree of continued conflict between former partners.

For the extended family, divorce disrupts grandparent–grandchild relationships and wider kinship networks. Grandparents on the non-resident parent’s side may lose contact with grandchildren entirely. The rise of divorce has also contributed significantly to the growth of lone parent families in the UK, since many divorces involve dependent children.

Serial monogamy describes the practice of having a succession of monogamous relationships or marriages — one at a time. As divorce has become more socially acceptable, more people go on to form new partnerships and remarry after divorce. Some functionalists interpret this as evidence that marriage as an institution remains highly valued: people seek it again after it breaks down rather than abandoning the institution entirely. Sociologists describe the growing prevalence of serial monogamy as reflecting the individualisation of relationship choice in contemporary society.

An empty shell marriage, by contrast, is a marriage that persists legally but in which the couple have effectively separated emotionally. Empty shell marriages may persist for financial reasons (such as maintaining a joint mortgage), social reasons (religious objection to divorce) or for the perceived benefit of children. This concept is important because it shows that official divorce statistics undercount the real number of relationships that have broken down.

Functionalist view: Parsons argued that the family adapts to meet social needs. Rising divorce rates may reflect rising expectations of what marriage should provide rather than signalling a crisis of the family. High remarriage rates support this: marriage as an institution remains valued, even if individual marriages fail.

Feminist view: Most divorce petitions are filed by women, supporting the feminist argument that marriage has historically placed greater burdens on women. Rising divorce rates reflect women’s growing economic independence and their capacity to leave unsatisfactory relationships. From this perspective, rising divorce is not a symptom of social breakdown but of women’s liberation from patriarchal constraints.

Marxist view: Marxists argue the causes of marital breakdown are often rooted in the economic conditions of capitalism — poverty, financial stress, the alienation of work and housing insecurity all increase pressure on family relationships. Zaretsky would see rising divorce as partly a consequence of the pressures capitalism places on workers and their families.

New Right view: Murray’s New Right perspective is critical of rising divorce rates, arguing that the growth of lone parent families resulting from divorce contributes to a dependency culture and the development of an underclass. Children raised without two parents are argued by the New Right to be educationally and socially disadvantaged. This view is challenged by feminist sociologists, who argue it pathologises lone parent families without addressing the structural causes of their difficulties.

Key Fact

The main consequences of divorce include: financial hardship (particularly for women); social isolation (particularly for men); varied impacts on children’s wellbeing; disruption of extended family relationships; and a significant increase in lone parent families. Serial monogamy and empty shell marriages show the complex reality behind divorce statistics.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
On a 4-mark Describe question about reasons for rising divorce rates, structure your answer using the four causes: legal change (Divorce Reform Act 1969 and the 2022 no-fault reform), secularisation (declining religious stigma), changing social attitudes (rising expectations of marriage) and the changing status of women (greater economic independence). One mark per well-described cause is the typical mark distribution, so covering all four secures full marks.

On a 12-mark Evaluate about divorce, never present rising rates as inherently a social problem — that is the New Right view (Murray), not an authorial claim. Present the New Right as one perspective alongside the feminist view (rising divorce reflects women’s independence) and the functionalist view (the institution of marriage remains valued). Explicitly compare these perspectives and reach a supported judgement. Students who list causes without engaging with perspectives or reaching a conclusion stay well below the Mastering band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Divorce rates in Britain rose dramatically from the 1970s, driven by legal change (Divorce Reform Act 1969; 2022 no-fault divorce reform in England and Wales), secularisation, changing social attitudes and the growing economic independence of women. Since the 1990s rates have slightly declined, partly because marriage is less common.
  • Consequences of divorce include: financial hardship (especially for women); social isolation (especially for men); varied impacts on children’s wellbeing; disruption of extended family relationships; and the significant growth of lone parent families. Empty shell marriages and serial monogamy show the complex social reality behind official divorce statistics.
  • Perspectives differ: functionalists (Parsons) see rising rates as reflecting changing expectations, not family collapse; feminists see them as evidence of women’s growing independence; Marxists link marital breakdown to economic pressures; the New Right (Murray) views rising divorce and lone parenthood as contributing to an underclass and social problems.
